steps.title: Pick the Real Problem
steps.narration: AJ starts the final week by choosing one problem that still feels real in his chest, not just one that sounds impressive on a slide. He wants the presentation to begin with a lived frustration people can recognize right away.

steps.title: Frame It Honestly
steps.narration: Nia cuts out every exaggerated claim and rewrites the setup so the crew names the actual user, the actual pain point, and the actual limit of what their solution can do. If the explanation is honest, the audience can trust the rest.

steps.title: Show the Proof Trail
steps.narration: Malik lays out the evidence trail: the questions they asked, the comments and examples they collected, and the pattern that kept showing up. The point is not to drown people in data. The point is to show that the build came from proof, not guessing.

steps.title: Walk Through the Build
steps.narration: AJ and Malik turn the messy building process into a clean story: first prompt, rough prototype, broken version, feedback, and stronger revision. Now the audience can see the workflow instead of imagining magic.

steps.title: Shape the Presentation Arc
steps.narration: With the facts in place, the crew shapes the final talk into one clear arc: here is the problem, here is what we learned, here is what we built, and here is why it matters. Week 4 is not about sounding polished. It is about making the learning visible.

steps.title: Open With the Hook
steps.narration: AJ practices opening with the exact moment the problem became impossible to ignore. That hook matters because it reminds the audience that the capstone began in real life, not in a random assignment prompt.

steps.title: Stress-Test Every Claim
steps.narration: Nia listens like a tough editor. Every time the crew says always, everyone, or best, she stops them and asks for proof. If they cannot defend a claim with evidence from the project, it does not make the final version.

steps.title: Make the Demo Safe
steps.narration: Malik gets the live demo ready by checking the flow, saving screenshots, and preparing a backup path in case the internet acts strange. A strong presentation is not only about confidence. It is about planning for reality.

steps.title: Practice in Front of People
steps.narration: The crew runs the talk for a small practice audience and listens for the moment people lean in, get confused, or ask follow-up questions. That reaction becomes feedback they can actually use before the final presentation.

steps.title: Revise for Clarity
steps.narration: AJ tightens the hook, Nia cleans the logic, and Malik sharpens the demo sequence. The final version is stronger because they tested it in public first. That is the Week 4 move: test, sharpen, present.

steps.title: Lead With Evidence of Learning
steps.narration: When the portfolio comes together, Malik makes sure it leads with evidence: the problem statement, the research trail, the build decisions, and the finished capstone. The portfolio is not decoration. It is proof that the crew can solve real problems.

steps.title: Tell the Story With Confidence
steps.narration: AJ presents without apologizing for what is unfinished. He focuses on what the crew learned, what the tool does right now, and why the problem was worth solving. Confidence here means ownership, not pretending the work is perfect.

steps.title: Answer Questions Honestly
steps.narration: Nia handles tough questions by staying grounded. If the answer is known, she gives it plainly. If the answer is not known yet, she says what the crew would test next. Honest answers make the presentation stronger than fake certainty ever could.

steps.title: Show the Workflow
steps.narration: Malik opens the repo, the prompts, and the working demo to show the actual workflow behind the final product. The audience gets to see that this crew does not just talk about ideas. They can document, build, and iterate in public.

steps.title: Leave as Problem Solvers
steps.narration: By the end, AJ, Nia, and Malik are not framed as kids who completed a course. They are framed as problem solvers who can notice a need, investigate it, build a response, and explain their thinking. That is the real graduation moment.

questions.question: Why does AJ start the presentation with a real problem instead of the most impressive-sounding one?
options: Real problems are easier to explain and defend with evidence
Impressive problems are usually too easy
Teachers only like personal examples
Real problems require less research
questions.explanation: A real problem gives the crew a concrete opening and stronger evidence. The audience can feel that the project came from lived experience rather than hype.

questions.question: What is Nia protecting when she removes exaggerated claims from the presentation?
options: The runtime of the slideshow
The technical depth of the repo
The audience's trust in the story
AJ's confidence on stage
questions.explanation: Honest framing makes the rest of the project credible. If the opening claims are shaky, the audience doubts everything else.

questions.question: Why does Malik show the proof trail instead of every piece of research the crew collected?
options: Because the audience only cares about the final tool
Because a selective evidence trail shows how the build came from proof rather than guessing
Because the crew forgot most of their research
Because screenshots are easier than data
questions.explanation: The goal is to show the logic of the project, not flood people with raw data. The evidence trail shows how the team moved from problem to build.

questions.question: What does Nia do when the crew uses big claims like 'everyone' or 'best' during practice?
options: She leaves them in to make the project sound stronger
She replaces them with proof-backed language or cuts them
She turns them into jokes
She moves them to the end of the talk
questions.explanation: Week 4 is about sharpening the story. Claims that cannot be defended with project evidence do not survive rehearsal.

questions.question: Why does Malik prepare screenshots and a backup path for the demo?
options: Because the final product is unfinished
Because planning for real conditions is part of a strong presentation
Because screenshots are more interesting than live demos
Because audiences prefer static slides
questions.explanation: A good presentation accounts for reality. Backup materials protect the story if live conditions go sideways.

questions.question: What is the value of practicing in front of a small audience before the final presentation?
options: It guarantees everyone will like the capstone
It creates usable feedback about confusion, interest, and pacing
It makes the final presentation unnecessary
It replaces testing the actual tool
questions.explanation: Practice reveals where people lean in or get lost. That reaction helps the crew sharpen the final talk.

questions.question: What should the portfolio lead with in Week 4?
options: Decorative screenshots and polished colors
Evidence of learning, problem framing, and build decisions
A long biography of the presenter
Every file in the repository
questions.explanation: The portfolio is proof, not decoration. It should show how the crew thought, researched, built, and learned.

questions.question: What makes Nia's approach to tough audience questions strong?
options: She answers every question with total certainty
She keeps answers honest and points to the next test when the crew does not know yet
She avoids questions that sound critical
She turns questions back on the audience
questions.explanation: Honest answers build trust. Saying what you know and what you would test next is stronger than fake certainty.

questions.question: Why does Malik show the repo and workflow during the portfolio presentation?
options: To prove the crew can document, build, and iterate in public
To make the presentation longer
To hide weaknesses in the demo
To avoid explaining the problem
questions.explanation: Showing the workflow makes the learning visible. It proves the team can move from idea to documented build process.
